title: Medeae fuga
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Pronunciation follows reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin.
about: Medea escapes punishment by taking to the air on her winged serpents, and Ovid turns the flight into a survey of Greece seen from above. Place after place is named for the transformation that happened there: a man carried on wings above Deucalion's flood, women of Cos who wore horns, a boy who leapt from a rock and became a swan, a mother who wept herself into a pool. At Ephyre, the old name of Corinth, the catalogue halts for four lines on the burning of Jason's new bride and the killing of Medea's sons, and then carries her to the citadel of Athens, where Aegeus takes her in and makes her his wife.

sentences.t:
Quod nisi pennatis serpentibus isset in auras,
non exempta foret poenae.
sentences.l: But if she had not gone off into the airs on winged serpents, she would not have been exempted from punishment.
sentences.i: Had she not gone up into the air behind her winged serpents, she would not have got clear of punishment.
sentences.n: Quod opens the sentence as a connecting relative used adverbially, roughly “and as to that”, which English carries with a plain “but”. isset (for iisset) and foret (for esset) are the two halves of a past condition contrary to fact: because the flight did happen, the punishment did not. poenae is a dative of separation with exempta, “taken out of punishment”.

sentences.t:
Fugit alta superque
Pelion umbrosum, Philyreia tecta, superque
Othryn et eventu veteris loca nota Cerambi.
sentences.l: She flees over the heights, and over shady Pelion, the Philyreian dwellings, and over Othrys and the places made known by the outcome of ancient Cerambus.
sentences.i: She flees high above, over shadowy Pelion and Philyra's halls, over Othrys and the country famous for what became of Cerambus long ago.
sentences.n: Fugit is present, the historic present, which sets the flight in front of the reader as it happens; the catalogue that follows keeps this tense (relinquit, transit, videt, respicit). alta is a neuter plural accusative of the space crossed, “the high places”. Philyreia tecta is the cave of Chiron, whose mother was Philyra. eventu is an ablative of cause with nota, “known through the outcome”.

sentences.t:
Hic ope nympharum sublatus in aera pennis,
cum gravis infuso tellus foret obruta ponto,
Deucalioneas effugit inobrutus undas.
sentences.l: He, lifted into the air on wings by the help of the nymphs, when the heavy earth had been buried under the sea poured over it, escaped, unburied, the Deucalionian waves.
sentences.i: He it was who, lifted into the air on wings by the nymphs' help, at the time when the whole weight of earth lay buried under the inpouring sea, came through Deucalion's waters unburied.
sentences.n: Hic picks up Cerambus from the line before. aera is a Greek accusative of aer. The cum-clause with the subjunctive foret obruta supplies the circumstances of the escape. Ovid sets obruta against inobrutus in the same sentence: the earth buried, the man not. Deucalioneas undas is the flood Deucalion survived.

sentences.t:
Aeoliam Pitanen a laeva parte relinquit
factaque de saxo longi simulacra draconis,
sentences.l: She leaves Aeolian Pitane on the left side, and the likenesses of a long serpent made out of stone,
sentences.i: She leaves Aeolian Pitane on her left, and the stone image of the long snake,
sentences.n: Pitanen is a Greek accusative. simulacra is a plural standing for a single image, an ordinary poetic liberty. relinquit governs a list that runs on well past this unit: everything that follows is one more thing she leaves behind her.

sentences.t:
Idaeumque nemus, quo nati furta, iuvencum
occuluit Liber falsi sub imagine cervi,
sentences.l: and the Idaean grove, in which Liber hid his son's theft, a bullock, under the appearance of a false stag,
sentences.i: and the grove on Ida, where Liber hid what his son had stolen, a bullock, under the shape of a deer that was not one,
sentences.n: furta is a plural for a singular, “the stolen thing”, and iuvencum stands in apposition to it, naming what was stolen. quo is an ablative of place, “in which”. falsi cervi is a genitive with imagine: the bullock was given the look of a stag that did not exist.

sentences.t:
quaque pater Corythi parva tumulatus harena est,
et quos Maera novo latratu terruit agros,
sentences.l: and where the father of Corythus was entombed in a little sand, and the fields which Maera terrified with a strange barking,
sentences.i: and the place where Corythus's father lies buried under a thin cover of sand, and the fields that Maera terrified with a barking never heard before,
sentences.n: quaque is the adverb “and where”. In quos ... terruit agros the noun agros has been pulled inside its own relative clause, which Latin does freely and English cannot, so the translation sets it back outside. novo latratu is an ablative of means, and novus here is “strange, new to the ear” rather than “recent”.

sentences.t:
Eurypylique urbem, qua Coae cornua matres
gesserunt tum cum discederet Herculis agmen
Phoebeamque Rhodon et Ialysios Telchinas,
sentences.l: and the city of Eurypylus, where the Coan mothers bore horns at that time when the company of Hercules was departing, and Phoeban Rhodes and the Ialysian Telchines,
sentences.i: and Eurypylus's city, where the women of Cos wore horns at the time Hercules's band was sailing away, and Rhodes that belongs to the Sun, and the Telchines of Ialysus,
sentences.n: cornua matres gesserunt is “the mothers wore horns”: the women of Cos were turned into cattle. tum cum is “at that time when”, with discederet subjunctive inside the cum-clause. Rhodon is a Greek accusative, and Phoebeam marks Rhodes as the Sun-god's island.

sentences.t:
quorum oculos ipso vitiantes omnia visu
Iuppiter exosus fraternis subdidit undis.
sentences.l: whose eyes, spoiling all things by the very sight, Jupiter loathed, and sank them beneath his brother's waves.
sentences.i: Jupiter loathed their eyes, which blighted everything by the mere look of them, and sank the Telchines beneath his brother's waters.
sentences.n: exosus is a perfect participle with an active sense, “having come to hate”, and it governs the accusative quorum oculos. subdidit is then left with no object expressed: the Telchines themselves are understood from the relative. ipso ... visu is an ablative of means, “by the sight itself”. fraternis undis is the sea, Neptune being Jupiter's brother.

sentences.t:
Transit et antiquae Cartheia moenia Ceae,
qua pater Alcidamas placidam de corpore natae
miraturus erat nasci potuisse columbam.
sentences.l: She crosses also the Cartheian walls of ancient Cea, where the father Alcidamas was going to marvel that a gentle dove had been able to be born from his daughter's body.
sentences.i: She crosses the walls of Carthaea on old Ceos too, where Alcidamas the father would live to wonder that a quiet dove could be born out of his daughter's body.
sentences.n: et here is “also” and does not join two verbs. miraturus erat is a future participle with erat, “was going to marvel”: the wonder is still ahead at the moment of the flight. nasci potuisse columbam is the indirect statement depending on it, with columbam as its accusative subject and potuisse as the infinitive.

sentences.t:
Inde lacus Hyries videt et Cycneia tempe,
quae subitus celebravit olor.
sentences.l: From there she sees the lake of Hyrie and the Cycnean vale, which a sudden swan made famous.
sentences.i: From there she sees Hyrie's lake and the valley of Cycnus, which a swan, appearing all at once, made famous.
sentences.n: tempe is an indeclinable Greek neuter plural used here as a common noun for a valley, which is why the relative quae is plural. subitus is an adjective where English wants an adverb: the swan is called sudden, meaning that it appeared on a sudden. Hyries is a Greek genitive.

sentences.l: For Phyllius there, at the command of the boy, had handed over birds and a wild lion, tamed;
sentences.i: For it was there that Phyllius, at the boy's bidding, delivered up birds and a wild lion, all of them broken to hand;
sentences.n: imperio is an ablative, “by the order of”. domitos is masculine plural and covers both volucres, which is feminine, and leonem: when one Latin adjective covers a mixed group it goes masculine. The boy is Cycnus, whose valley was named two lines above, and the tasks are a lover's proofs.

sentences.t:
taurum quoque vincere iussus
vicerat, et spreto totiens iratus amore
praemia poscenti taurum suprema negabat.
sentences.l: ordered to overcome a bull as well, he had overcome it; and, angered because his love had been scorned so many times, he kept refusing the bull, the last of the prizes, to the one demanding it.
sentences.i: Ordered to master a bull as well, he had mastered it; and then, stung by a love spurned so many times over, he kept the bull back, the last prize of all, from the boy who kept demanding it.
sentences.n: quoque here is the plain adverb “also”. iussus is a passive participle, “having been ordered”, with the infinitive vincere depending on it. spreto ... amore is an ablative of cause with iratus, “angry because his love had been scorned”. taurum sits in apposition to praemia suprema, “the last prizes”, and poscenti is a dative participle standing for the boy who was asking.

sentences.t:
Ille indignatus “cupies dare” dixit et alto
desiluit saxo.
sentences.l: He, indignant, said “you will want to give it,” and leapt down from a high rock.
sentences.i: Outraged, he said, “You will want to give it,” and flung himself down from a high rock.
sentences.n: cupies is a future: the boy's threat is that Phyllius will soon be desperate to hand the bull over, when it is too late to. alto ... saxo is an ablative of separation split around its verb, a favourite arrangement in the hexameter.

sentences.t:
Cuncti cecidisse putabant:
factus olor niveis pendebat in aere pennis.
sentences.l: All were thinking that he had fallen: made a swan, he was hanging in the air on snowy wings.
sentences.i: Everyone thought he had fallen to his death; but, turned into a swan, he was hanging in the air on snow-white wings.
sentences.n: cecidisse is an indirect statement after putabant with its accusative subject left unexpressed, “that he had fallen”. cadere does double duty, to fall and to fall dead, and the whole point of the line turns on it. The colon sets what everyone believed against what was actually in the air.

sentences.t:
At genetrix Hyrie, servatum nescia, flendo
delicuit stagnumque suo de nomine fecit.
sentences.l: But the mother Hyrie, not knowing him saved, melted away by weeping and made a pool from her own name.
sentences.i: But his mother Hyrie, with no idea he had been saved, dissolved away in weeping and made a pool that took its name from her.
sentences.n: nescia normally takes a genitive; Magnus prints servatum, which is accusative, best read with esse understood, “not knowing him to have been saved”, while some editions print servati, the ordinary genitive. Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. flendo is an ablative gerund, “by weeping”.

sentences.t:
Adiacet his Pleuron, in qua trepidantibus alis
Ophias effugit natorum vulnera Combe.
sentences.l: Pleuron lies next to these, in which Combe, the daughter of Ophius, escaped on trembling wings the wounds of her sons.
sentences.i: Next to these lies Pleuron, where Combe, Ophius's daughter, escaped her sons' blows on trembling wings.
sentences.n: his is a dative with adiacet, “lies alongside these”. Ophias is a Greek patronymic in apposition to Combe, “the daughter of Ophius”. natorum is a subjective genitive with vulnera: the wounds are the ones her own sons meant to deal her.

sentences.t:
Inde Calaureae Letoidos adspicit arva,
in volucrem versi cum coniuge conscia regis.
sentences.l: From there she looks upon the fields of Leto's-daughter's Calaurea, aware of a king turned into a bird together with his wife.
sentences.i: From there she looks down on the fields of Calaurea, ground that belongs to Leto's daughter and knows of a king turned into a bird, and his wife with him.
sentences.n: conscia is a neuter plural agreeing with arva: the fields themselves are in the know, and what they know is given by the genitive versi regis, “of a king turned”. Letoidos is a Greek genitive. adspicit keeps the older unassimilated spelling of aspicit, which this edition preserves. Ovid names neither the king nor his wife; the ground is made to remember them instead.

sentences.t:
Dextera Cyllene est, in qua cum matre Menephron
concubiturus erat saevarum more ferarum
sentences.l: On the right is Cyllene, on which Menephron was going to lie with his mother in the manner of savage beasts.
sentences.i: On the right stands Cyllene, where Menephron was to bed his own mother after the fashion of savage beasts.
sentences.n: Dextera is a predicate adjective doing an adverb's work, “on the right”. concubiturus erat is the future participle with erat again, “was going to lie with”: as with Alcidamas above, the deed is still ahead at the moment of the flight. more is an ablative, “in the manner of”. The edition sets no stop after ferarum, although the sentence plainly ends there; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t:
Cephison procul hinc deflentem fata nepotis
respicit, in tumidam phocen ab Apolline versi,
Eumelique domum lugentis in aere natum.
sentences.l: She looks back at Cephisos, far from here weeping over the fate of his grandson, turned by Apollo into a swollen seal, and at the house of Eumelus, mourning his son in the air.
sentences.i: She looks back at Cephisus, far off, weeping for the fate of the grandson Apollo had turned into a bloated seal, and at the house of Eumelus, who grieves for a son now in the air.
sentences.n: Cephison and phocen are Greek accusatives. versi is a genitive participle agreeing with nepotis: it is the grandson who was turned, not Cephisos. lugentis likewise agrees with Eumeli, so it is the man who mourns, though the phrase names his house. in aere natum, “a son in the air”, is how Ovid says the boy is now a bird.

sentences.t:
Tandem vipereis Ephyren Pirenida pennis
contigit.
sentences.l: At last on viperous wings she touched Pirenian Ephyre.
sentences.i: At last, on her serpents' wings, she reached Ephyre of Pirene.
sentences.n: Ephyren is a Greek accusative and Pirenida a Greek accusative adjective formed from the spring Pirene: Ephyre is the old name of Corinth, and the spring says which Ephyre is meant. vipereis pennis are the wings of the winged serpents that draw her car.

sentences.t:
Hic aevo veteres mortalia primo
corpora vulgarunt pluvialibus edita fungis.
sentences.l: Here in the first age the men of old spread it abroad that mortal bodies had come forth from rainy mushrooms.
sentences.i: Here in the earliest age the old inhabitants put it about that human bodies had sprung from mushrooms brought up by rain.
sentences.n: vulgarunt is a syncopated form of vulgaverunt. What they put about is an indirect statement with esse left out: corpora is its accusative subject and edita stands for edita esse. pluvialibus fungis is an ablative of source, and aevo primo an ablative of time.

sentences.t:
Sed postquam Colchis arsit nova nupta venenis,
flagrantemque domum regis mare vidit utrumque,
sentences.l: But after the new bride blazed with Colchian poisons, and each sea saw the house of the king on fire,
sentences.i: But after the new bride went up in flames from Colchian poisons, and both seas saw the king's palace burning,
sentences.n: Colchis here is not the noun “the Colchian woman” but the ablative plural of the adjective agreeing with venenis, “with Colchian drugs”; the trap is real, since the Colchian woman is standing in the sentence. Ovid does not name the new bride. mare utrumque, “each sea”, is the pair of gulfs the city stands between, and the fire was visible from both.

sentences.t:
sanguine natorum perfunditur impius ensis,
ultaque se male mater Iasonis effugit arma.
sentences.l: the unholy sword is drenched with the blood of her sons, and the mother, having avenged herself wickedly, escaped the arms of Jason.
sentences.i: the unholy sword is drenched with her sons' blood, and the mother, having taken a wicked revenge, escaped Jason's weapons.
sentences.n: ulta is a deponent participle: passive in form, active in sense, “having avenged herself”. male goes with it and means “wickedly, to her own ruin”, matching impius on the sword; both words are the poet's judgment, not the mother's. perfunditur is a present inside past narrative, and it makes the sword, not the mother, the subject of the killing, which is given half a line and no more. effugit can be read as present or perfect, the form being the same.

sentences.t:
Hinc Titaniacis ablata draconibus intrat
Palladias arces,
sentences.l: From here, carried off by Titanian dragons, she enters the Palladian citadels,
sentences.i: From here, borne away by her Titan-descended dragons, she enters the citadel of Pallas,
sentences.n: Titaniacis marks the serpents as belonging to the stock of the Titans, the family Medea comes from on her father's side. ablata is a passive participle, “having been carried off”. Palladias arces is Athens, named from its goddess, with the plural arces standing for the one citadel.

sentences.t:
quae te, iustissima Phene,
teque, senex Peripha, pariter videre volantes
innixamque novis neptem Polypemonis alis.
sentences.l: which saw you, most just Phene, and you, aged Periphas, flying alike, and the granddaughter of Polypemon leaning upon new wings.
sentences.i: and the citadel saw you, most just Phene, and you, old Periphas, flying side by side, and Polypemon's granddaughter propped on wings that were new to her.
sentences.n: videre is the poetic third-person plural perfect for viderunt; -ere is a standard alternative to the -erunt ending, and the two are the same tense. quae takes up arces as its subject. Ovid then breaks off from his narrative to speak to Phene and Periphas directly, te ... teque, the turn aside called apostrophe. volantes is accusative plural covering the two of them, while innixam is accusative singular with neptem.

sentences.t:
Excipit hanc Aegeus, facto dammandus in uno;
nec satis hospitium est: thalami quoque foedere iungit.
sentences.l: Aegeus takes her in, to be condemned in one deed only; and the hospitality is not enough: he joins her also by the bond of the marriage-chamber.
sentences.i: Aegeus takes her in, a man to be condemned for this one act alone; and shelter was not enough for him: he bound her to himself by marriage as well.
sentences.n: dammandus stands in the edition with a doubled m; the word the sense requires is damnandus, the gerundive of damno, “deserving condemnation”, and other editions print it so. Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. facto ... in uno is an ablative with in, “in one deed”, and the gerundive marks Aegeus as blameable for that act and no other. iungit has no object expressed: hanc, Medea, is carried over from the line before. quoque is once more the plain adverb “also”, not a form of quisque.
